rows.subtype: Stage 3: The target's confusion and shame [Receiver]
rows.description: The child feels stomach aches before school, thinks it is his fault and hides it from parents for fear of making things worse. Fear and shame make bullying secret, which helps it continue.
graph_context: previous stage: Testing with small acts
next stage: The bystanders' dilemma
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: fear, shame, confusion

rows.description: Classmates feel sorry but fear being next, some laugh to stay safe, and a few even join. Each waits for someone else to act, so a group of kind children can still allow harm.
graph_context: previous stage: The target's confusion and shame
next stage: An ally breaks the silence
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: amusement, fear, trust

rows.subtype: Stage 5: An ally breaks the silence [Response]
rows.description: One child sits beside the target, says "come play with us" and tells a teacher afterwards. Standing with the target, and telling an adult, is not tale-telling; it is safe and brave, and it changes the group's mood.
graph_context: previous stage: The bystanders' dilemma
next stage: Adults act on both sides
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: trust

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
rows.description: The school protects the target, is firm with the bully and also asks what unmet need drives him. The child who bullied needs consequence and support to learn other ways of getting respect.
graph_context: previous stage: An ally breaks the silence
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17
related mind states: admiration

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Status and a group's approval [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager who wants to be at the top of the social order finds that mocking someone draws laughs from the group. Group approval is a powerful reward at this age, more so than the target's suffering is a deterrent.
graph_context: next stage: Escalation online and offline
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12
related mind states: amusement

rows.description: Mocking moves to edited photos, fake accounts and exclusion from plans. Screens create distance from the victim's face, so cruelty feels lighter to the sender and heavier to the receiver.
graph_context: previous stage: Status and a group's approval
next stage: The target's withdrawal
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12

rows.description: The teen stops speaking in class, eats alone and sleeps badly, and may say he is fine. Bullying works by isolating, and the sharpest pain is often the belief that nobody would believe or help.
graph_context: previous stage: Escalation online and offline
next stage: The bystander's moral tension
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12
related mind states: detachment, loneliness, hurt

rows.description: A classmate feels guilt for laughing once and fear of being targeted if she stops. Small acts such as messaging the target privately or refusing to share the post are real help, and do not require confronting the bully in public.
graph_context: previous stage: The target's withdrawal
next stage: Reporting and evidence
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12
related mind states: amusement, fear, guilt
possibly related concept (heuristic): Allyship and how to help a targeted person

rows.description: The target or an ally saves screenshots and tells a parent, teacher or counsellor, who takes it seriously. Reporting is protection and not weakness, and adults must act without making the target pay for having spoken.
graph_context: previous stage: The bystander's moral tension
next stage: Accountability and repair
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12

rows.description: The bully faces consequences and a chance to understand harm, ideally with help for what drives the behaviour. The target gets support to regain confidence, and a bystander group learns that silence has a cost.
graph_context: previous stage: Reporting and evidence
this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12
